sources.citation: Sinha, Kali Prasad. 1981. The Bishnupriya Manipuri Language. Calcutta: Firma KLM. x+119 pp. (published revision of the 1968 Jadavpur PhD thesis; the source the earlier scan named as unreachable -- now found open on archive.org)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: No accent/stress section. Ch. III 'Sounds' (pp. 20-32) is purely segmental; Ch. IV-IX are historical phonology. The only placement-related remarks are diachronic (pp. 40-41): syncope 'due to strong stress on the initial vowel', aphesis 'when a medial vowel is stressed'; plus syntactic 'stress' = emphasis by word order (pp. 114-115). Voiced aspirates > plain voiced + glottal closure noted (p. 24).

sources.citation: Sinha, Kali Prasad. 1998. Bishnupriya Manipuri Byakaran [grammar written in Bishnupriya Manipuri, Bengali script].
sources.note: p. 17: long i/u do not exist; what is sometimes taken for a long vowel is really a short vowel bearing shvasaghat (stress), e.g. nilmani, murgo. p. ~129: defines stress generally (the syllable uttered with more breath force gains prominence) and says a stressed syllable causes weakening/loss of vowels in other syllables (aphesis/syncope/apocope). Also sentence-level 'stress' on constituents. No rule for which syllable carries word stress.

sources.citation: Sinha, K. P. 1986. An Etymological Dictionary of Bishnupriya Manipuri. Calcutta: Punthi Pustak.
sources.note: Sign list (p. xv): an acute 'above or after a vowel indicates stress'; inspection of entries (e.g. Á- 'to be' < bhava-, ÁKAR- 'begin' < Mt. hau-) shows the mark flags the glottal-constriction reflex of lost h/voiced aspirates, i.e. a lexical feature, not positional word stress. Introduction has no accent statement.
